CausalChain: HCC cells secrete tryptophan metabolites via exosomes → These metabolites activate AHR in TAMs → AHR activation triggers metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic modifications in TAMs → Downregulation of co‐stimulatory/antigen‐presenting molecules and upregulation of immunosuppressive cytokines → Inefficient activation and recruitment of CD8+ T cells → Enhanced immune evasion and tumor progression
Hypothesis: In HCC, tumor‐derived tryptophan metabolites drive AHR‐dependent metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming in TAMs that suppresses CD8+ T cell function. Inhibiting the AHR pathway in TAMs will reprogram them towards an immunostimulatory phenotype, restore effective T cell responses, and improve the outcomes of immune checkpoint blockade therapies.
Abstract: We propose that in the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment, tumor‐derived metabolites—particularly those from the tryptophan catabolic pathway, conveyed via exosomes—activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) in tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs). This activation induces a metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming of the TAMs that results in the downregulation of co‐stimulatory and antigen‐presenting molecules, while upregulating immunosuppressive signals. Consequently, the reprogrammed TAMs promote CD8+ T cell dysfunction, ultimately facilitating tumor immune evasion and tumor progression. Targeting the AHR pathway in TAMs to reverse this metabolic reprogramming constitutes a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance anti‐PD1 and other immune therapies in liver cancer.
